HEADLINE: APA inks $500m pipeline deal for Narrabri gas
TEXT:
Santos' controversial Narrabri coal seam gas project in NSW is seeing the first signs of progress for years, with a deal signed with APA Group for gas transportation through a potential new $500 million pipeline.

The agreement is set to be followed by the long-awaited lodgement by Santos of the environmental impact statement for the Narrabri venture.

The proposed 450-kilometre line, the Western Slopes Pipeline, would run from the Narrabri fields to APA's existing pipeline between Moomba and Sydney.

It is still conditional on Santos giving the go-ahead for the CSG project, which faces strong opposition from some environmental groups and has been stalled for several years as the oil and gas producer cut spending.

APA chief executive Mick McCormack said the aim was to have environmental approvals in place by the end of 2018. A Santos spokesman could not comment.

But The Courier newspaper in Narrabri Shire quoted APA executive Bruce Clement in mid-January saying Santos was "committed to endeavouring to deliver" the project.

HEADLINE: Strong demand allows lenders to lift charges
TEXT:
Commonwealth Bank of Australia and other lenders are raising borrowing rates by up to 50 basis points, cutting discounts, reintroducing $600 administrative fees and revamping product ranges as strong buyer demand for property in Melbourne and Sydney enables lenders to offset rising costs and rebuild margins.

Other lenders are raising rates because of fears a demand surge could overwhelm their administrative systems and accelerate volumes to the regulatory speed limits.

CBA, the nation's biggest mortgage lender, is raising rates for the second time in two weeks and reintroducing some fees.

The bank is set to announce an increase of 47 basis points, or a rise to 4.73 per cent, on its three-year "special rate" investment loans. The rate on its owner-occupied "special rate" loan is rising by 30 basis points.

It is also reintroducing a $600 establishment fee, or $8 monthly loan service, for the special rate offers, starting immediately.

"From time to time we offer special discounts on select products," a bank spokesman said about new products.

"This week we informed our mortgage broking partners, that our existing three-year Special Rate Saver Offer has been replaced with new rates on our Extra Home Loan product, which offers a better rate when the introductory two year special discount expires than the existing Special Rate Saver product," he said.

Other big name lenders such as AMP Bank, a division of the nation's largest diversified financial conglomerate, and National Australia Bank, are revamping their product offerings. For example, AMP has pulled a 4.09 basis point offer on a three-year fixed rate and raised the rate to 4.59 basis points.

AMP recently announced it will no longer accept new refinance applications from property investors. NAB is withdrawing its Homeplus and Peak Performance products.

A NAB spokesman said that existing customers will not be disadvantaged and that it has increased the product range available through mortgage brokers.

Newcastle Permanent, which has a large deposit base to fund loans, is cutting the discount on its Premium Plus package of mortgage and credit products by 10 basis points to 43 basis points.

Last month it increased the cost of fixed rates on owner-occupied and investment loans from between 5 and 25 basis points for one to three years.

Australian First Mortgage, a non-bank lender, is also restructuring its product range and increasing four-year fixed rates by 50 per cent. 

Bank Australia, which uses retail deposits to fund lending, has reintroduced a $595 establishment fee on all home loans and has increased variable rates by 8 basis points.

"This is reflective of continued pressure for the bank to raise retail deposits in order to fund lending activity, which continues to be strong in recent months," a Bank Australia spokesman said. "We have seen an uptick in demand from investors over past weeks but we have not sought to offer incentives to attract more of this lending at this time as we are getting the growth we are seeking."

HEADLINE: Data sharing carries fraud risk, warns Elliott
TEXT:
The call by a parliamentary committee for the big banks to seamlessly provide financial data to customers will create a "real risk" of fraud if it is established too quickly, said the chief executive of ANZ Banking Group, Shayne Elliott.

The bank chief executives are expected to be questioned by the House of Representatives economics committee in hearings that start on Friday about their willingness to support a scheme that would allow customers to request data, which can then be used to shop around for a better deal.

The committee's first report in November imposed aggressive timelines for the creation of an "open data access regime" and suggested this should involve customers' transaction history, account balances, credit card usage, mortgage repayments and small business data. The committee, chaired by Liberal MP David Coleman, called for ASIC to create a "binding framework" to deliver the data via "application programming interfaces" [APIs] by July 2018. The recommendation was inspired by similar moves in Europe.

Speaking at the AltFi Australasia Summit in Sydney, where several fintechs argued better data access would allow them to compete more vigorously, Mr Elliott said he supported moves to provide data to customers. But he suggested more time may be needed to ensure a secure regime was created.

"It is our customers' data, we are a custodian of that data, we have a responsibility to look after it and protect it ... we do need to think about security and the way that that is undertaken," he said. "It does open up new risks. I am not suggesting that should mean we don't get into open data regimes, but it means we should be really thoughtful about it.

"I know people will criticise the banks, and say we are trying to slow that down. I don't think that is the motivation. I think it is literally looking after our customers. We all know people who have experienced fraud. If we open up data too quickly, there is real risk here and this needs to be thought through."

Fintech Australia, which represents start-ups, supports the creation of governance standards to allow for the safe transfer of banking data. The Productivity Commission is also expected to make recommendations for data to be opened up across the economy in a report to be delivered to the government in March.

Mr Elliott's warning on data security was backed by cloud accounting software maker Xero's head of financial services Ben Styles, who said a mid-2018 timeline for a open data regime could be ambitious.

"The investment that is required to do that securely - and we have been on that journey for 10 years - is significant," he told the event. "No financial institution is going to step into a situation where they are sharing that kind of information without a high level of security."

Mr Styles called for a better quality public debate about what kind of data customers want to be shared, suggesting that while opening access to transaction data had obvious benefits, insights that a bank had formed about a customer might not be appropriate for sharing. He said Xero's experience was that customer control was essential.

"When people think of an API, they think of a big pipeline that third parties can [use to] suck a whole bunch of insightful information. But giving customer control at a granular level [on what they share] is really important. We have been quite mindful about customer control ... that has allowed us to learn very quickly, but also very safely."

Adam Flesch, a principal at Oliver Wyman, said banks in Britain had embraced the creation of the country's "open banking standard", which has the support of the British government. The banks there realised they were already becoming exposed to risks of data being "scraped" off their account statements and were now involved in designing the British regime to protect their interests, he said.

HEADLINE: No relief as Slaters posts $425.1m loss
TEXT:
The tenure of Slater & Gordon's management and board will come under renewed scrutiny as lenders negotiate a recapitalisation plan to keep the troubled law firm afloat.

On Monday, Slater & Gordon posted a half-year loss of $425.1 million as managing director Andrew Grech conceded the United Kingdom turnaround plan was progressing at a "slower than anticipated" pace.

It comes as the personal injury law firm prepares to fight one of Australia's largest shareholder class actions and is the subject of a serious regulatory probe into its accounting practices. Its shareholders are braced for a near total wipe-out of their investment.

Slater & Gordon is in talks with its lenders about a recapitalisation plan that will most likely result in a debt for equity swap.

The listed law firm conceded earlier this month that because the size of its debt exceeded the value of the business, it relied on "the support of its lenders to continue as a going concern".

The half-year accounts, released Monday, show its liabilities exceed its assets by $126 million.

It is understood the primary concern among Slater & Gordon's debt financiers - who are set to inherit the company - is to stabilise what they believe is a sustainable business, and provide confidence to the staff and clients.

Slater & Gordon must present a plan to its lenders by the end of May. The company is likely to remain a listed entity after an agreement is reached with lenders to provide sufficient liquidity to them should their loans be converted to equity.

But lenders are likely to implement wholesale changes to the management and the board responsible for the large losses resulting from a doomed $1.3 billion acquisition of Quindell's professional services division in Britain in early 2015.

The half-year loss was affected by a further write-down of its United Kingdom assets of $350.3 million and the under-performance of its UK and Australian operations, which had until recently been a consistent performer.

Monday's write-down adds to the $1 billion in impairments taken in February 2016 and means the Quindell acquisition that Slater & Gordon heralded as transformational is now deemed worthless.

Mr Grech did tender his resignation to the board at the time of the first write-down, but the board led by chairman John Skippen decided he should stay to oversee the turnaround plan and negotiations with lenders.

The pair will now face a battle to convince lenders, who will be forced to book a loss on their loans, that they should remain in place. The law firm reported group revenue fell to $322.7 million from $487.5 million in the December 2016 interim period.

Cash flows remained negative at $11.4 million, an improvement from the negative $20.9 million outflow in the second half of 2016. Slater & Gordon said that cash flow was positive by $7.1 million if non-recurring restructuring and refinancing costs were added back.

The interim results showed the 82-year old Australian business was being hurt by what Mr Grech described as "negative publicity and sentiment".

Revenues in the Australian business fell by 17.5 per cent to $114.2 million with earnings, adjusted for changes in work in progress for the half year came in at 5.7 million, a 70 per cent decline from the corresponding half-year.

The accounts show the law firm slashed its advertising spend by more than half to $43.9 million (the company's equity is also currently valued at $44 million) while salaries fell to $167.2 million from $215.8 million.

In a blow to speculative investors betting on a change in fortunes, Slater & Gordon shares traded 20 per cent lower following the release at 12.5¢.

The company's shares have halved in value in since the start of 2017, but have fallen 98 per cent from their peak of about $8 in April 2015.

The company reminded beleaguered shareholders it was the subject of a fresh Australian Securities and Investment Commission investigation regarding its accounting.

Slater & Gordon said it was co-operating with the regulator, which has asked for documents relating to potential falsification of records, to ensure the investigation could be completed as soon as possible.

Slater & Gordon is also facing a $250 million shareholder class action led by rival class action firm Maurice Blackburn. The company said there were no assets, other than its insurance policies, available to meet the judgment.

HEADLINE: Comeback kid QBE's profits to accelerate
TEXT:
QBE chief executive John Neal says premium increases and more stringent underwriting will allow the global insurer's turnaround to accelerate, after solid profit growth in 2016 saw it boost its dividend and launch a $1 billion share buyback.

On a day when the $17 billion global insurer unveiled some of its best results in recent years, including a jump in profits and insurance margins, the news was largely overshadowed by Mr Neal's relationship with his personal assistant.

The QBE annual report released on Monday said that Mr Neal's short-term incentive was cut by 20 per cent, or about $550,000, because "some recent personal decisions by the CEO have been inconsistent with the board's expectations".

The annual report, which outlined the insurer's full-year results for the period ending December 31, revealed a company in much better shape than in preceding years.

QBE reported a 5 per cent increase in full-year net profit after tax to $US844 million ($1.1 billion) with return on equity of 8.1 per cent. Cash profit after tax also increased to $US898 million, compared with $US893 million a year ago, beating a $US769 million forecast of 13 analysts polled by Thomson Reuters.

Its insurance profit margin for the 12 months to December 31 rose 0.7 percentage points to 9.7 per cent, while adjusted profit - which strips out one-off costs and asset sales - rose 2.5 per cent to $US833 million.

QBE rewarded its patient shareholders with a $1 billion share buyback over three years and a 10 per cent increase in its full-year dividend to 33¢ per share, 50 per cent franked.

Commenting on the buyback, Mr Neal said the board had been mulling how best to reward shareholders for over a year as the insurer's remediation plans for the Australian and New Zealand divisions were implemented.

"It was only in February this year did we increase the dividend payout ratio up to 65 per cent and with the strength of the capital and the strength and confidence that the board has about our forward plans, we think we can deliver a bit more," he said.

"To increase the dividend payout is just not efficient with the credit we hold, so a buyback is just a better option."

Mr Neal said QBE would be "sensitive" to the share price and the book value of the company when deciding how many shares to buy back from investors over the three years.

"It's just about getting the balance and the timing right," he said.

CLSA analyst Jan van der Schalk welcomed the buyback. "This is a strong result from QBE, yet another iteration of the No. 1 cast-iron rule of insurance: shrink the book, grow the margin.

"The stand-out number is second-half 2016 margin of 11.23 per cent [excluding reserve releases], indicative of the underwriting turnaround John Neal and his team are crafting.

"Nothing dramatic in guidance going forward which, in and of itself, is a good thing - we like our insurers beige when the cycle is in its cheap phase."

The markets also reacted favourably and the stock was up about 4.5 per cent in early afternoon trading, finishing 2.4 per cent higher to hit $12.60, just shy of a 12-month high of $13.02 hit earlier this month.

QBE shares have gained 18.4 per cent in the past year, compared to a 17.3 per cent rise in the S&P/ASX 200 Index.

The result comes after the August 2016 announcement of "remediation" plans for the Australian and New Zealand divisions of the business after insurance margins in the regional business fell from 14.8 per cent in the first half of 2015 to 8.9 per cent in the first half of 2016.

Mr Neal told investors that while insurance remediation takes time, a combination of pricing increases, enhanced underwriting discipline and claims focus is expected to return the attritional claims ratio to more acceptable levels by the end of 2017.

"It's good to see a 3.4 per cent improvement in a half and I think one or two analysts have said that is remarkable. We've improved the attritional claims ratio at QBE in my time by 6 per cent. Few have done that," he said.

As well as improving its North American operations and undertaking a review in Latin America, QBE has divided the Australian and New Zealand operations into 44 "cells" with regular reviews undertaken for each cell.

It has also established underwriting hubs in Miami and Singapore, used data and analytics to assist with data-driven underwriting decisions, and rolled out a QBE Underwriting Academy to provide accreditation to its underwriters.

With global pricing being challenged over the last seven years, insurers have been struggling to hit their margins, with some increasing their premium prices.

QBE's Australian premium rates were up 1.7 per cent for the full year compared with a decline of 0.1 per cent at the half-year, including a fourth quarter increase of 4.5 per cent. The insurers increased CTP prices by about 18 per cent at the end of last year and Mr Neal said there may be more change as the NSW government's CTP reforms roll out.

"From our point of view the business is now within our expectations and performing in line with our expectations. Dependent on when or what the reforms looks like, will depend on how we will adjust our pricing," he said.

HEADLINE: Bellamy's chairman Woolley tipped to step down in deal
TEXT:
Bellamy's Australia chairman Rob Woolley is expected to announce plans to resign from the infant formula company at a shareholder meeting on Tuesday as part of a compromise deal that is expected to partially back rebel shareholder Jan Cameron's bid to roll four of the group's directors.

It is believed Mr Woolley has told investors about his intention to resign as early as Tuesday as Ms Cameron's two-month campaign to remove directors she believed were responsible for the company's operational problems comes to a head at an extraordinary shareholder meeting in Melbourne.

Mr Woolley was not included in Ms Cameron's original motion to spill the board but the Tasmanian entrepreneur later called for him to resign after the two old friends fell out. It has also emerged that David Baxby, a former Virgin Australia director and long-time lieutenant of British entrepreneur Richard Branson, has been tapped as a possible candidate to succeed Mr Woolley as chairman of the company.

Ms Cameron returned to Melbourne this week after meeting with the two overseas investors, which hold the balance of power in the tussle for board control, in the United States and Hong Kong.

It is believed Boston-based hedge fund Delta and a Hong Kong investment fund submitted an alternative proposal to install two of their own nominated directors but that motion was rejected by the board because it came too close to Tuesday's shareholder meeting and would have required Ms Cameron withdrawing her requisition. One of the people nominated was Mr Baxby, a highly regarded Australian businessman working abroad.

Ms Cameron had proposed unseating four independent directors, and installing herself along with two allies after the demise of company's fortunes. Sources said proxies indicated the final vote would be tight and Bellamy's had been canvassing retail shareholders repeatedly to muster support.

The two funds collectively control more than 13 per cent of the company. Ms Cameron is believed to control about 18 per cent of the company's issued capital through the Black Prince Foundation.

With the funds' support, Ms Cameron's proposal is expected to have backing from as much as 40 per cent of the company's shareholders. Two of her nominees, Rodd Peters and Chan Wai-Chan, are expected to be voted in as directors. Ms Cameron herself is not expected to be voted onto the board, however.

It is believed the two investment groups will vote in favour of the motions for Launa Inman and Michael Wadley, two of the four directors named in Ms Cameron's proposal, to step down. The investors are less critical of the two other directors, Patria Mann and Charles Sitch, because they joined the board in only March 2016. There is room for nine directors in total on the board.

The saga surrounding Bellamy's, which sacked its former chief Laura McBain and slashed its profit guidance in January, has raised corporate governance concerns about share trading in the company and questions around why the board was not on top of the company's operational problems.
